generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, feedback on your work is most useful when it changes your next piece. A comment such as 'you describe your material but do not evaluate it' is reviewed, interpreted into what evaluating would actually involve, articulated as a concrete action, and applied next time. Treated as a loop rather than a verdict, feedback is how work improves across any course of study.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who receive the same comment on a piece of work: their argument describes its material but does not evaluate it.

Student A reads the comment, feels the mark is harsh, and files the work away. On the next task the same comment returns. Student A reviewed the feedback but never interpreted it into an action or applied it, so nothing changed. The feedback was received, not used.

Student B reads the comment, works out what evaluating would look like, and writes it as a concrete action: question each source before using it. On the next task Student B does exactly that, and the comment does not return. The cycle has closed: review, interpret, articulate, apply.

Both were given the same feedback. Only Student B fed it forward, and only Student B's work improved because of it.
generatedProse.summary: The feedback cycle turns comments into improvement through four stages: review, interpret, articulate and apply. Run as a self-directed loop with a growth mindset, it closes only when your next piece of work shows the change. You can now describe the cycle, judge how well a student used feedback, and plan how to feed your own feedback forward. Together with the earlier lessons, you now own the learning, assessment and feedback cycle.

check.body: Why does one student's work improve from feedback when another's does not?

items.text: They interpret the comment into a concrete action and apply it to the next piece of work.
They disagree with the mark more strongly.
They receive more detailed feedback than others.
They keep the feedback filed for later reference.

feedback.correct: That's right. Interpreting the comment into an action and applying it is what closes the loop and improves the work.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what is done with the same comment.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Work improves when the comment is interpreted into a concrete action and applied next time. The same feedback, filed or merely disputed, changes nothing.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
